Thank you for the opportunity to revise our manuscript. We have addressed every
comment from you and both reviewers point-by-point below. Reviewer comments
appear in red boxes, our replies in blue boxes, verbatim text from the revised
manuscript in grey boxes, and the resulting changes in green boxes. All page
numbers refer to the revised manuscript with tracked changes.

<!-- The summary div is replaced at render with a linked list of every comment
     that carries a summary="..." attribute, together with its status. Place it
     where the summary belongs — conventionally right after this opening. Give
     summary= only to the comments you want surfaced at the top. Instead of the
     div you can set `summary: true` under response-letter: in the YAML header
     (inserts it before the first section); `summary: false` suppresses it. -->

::: {.response-summary}
:::

<!-- {.editor} starts the editor section: comments here are numbered E.1, E.2, …
     with anchors #cmt-E-1. Put it before the reviewers. A `.comment .general`
     is an unnumbered overall remark; a plain `.comment` in this section is the
     first numbered editor point (E.1). -->

# Editor {.editor}

::: {.comment .general}
Both reviewers find the question timely and the design sound. They converge,
however, on the analysis: the sample-size justification and the robustness of
the central effect both need strengthening before the paper can be accepted.
:::

::: {.reply}
We thank the editor for handling our manuscript and for the concise synthesis
of the reviews. We have strengthened both points the reviewers raise: the
sample size is now justified by an a priori power analysis (see
[Comment 1.1](#cmt-1-1)), and the central effect is reported under three
analytic choices (see [Comment 1.2](#cmt-1-2)).
:::

::: {.comment summary="data and analysis scripts made openly available"}
Please confirm that the data and analysis scripts are available, and state
where, in line with the journal's open-science policy.
:::

::: {.reply status="done"}
The data and analysis scripts are openly available on the OSF (link in the
manuscript). We now state this in a Data Availability statement (p. 18).
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

<!-- {{< pagebreak >}} breaks the page in PDF and DOCX and is ignored in HTML.
     Conventionally one between reviewers. Each plain `# Reviewer N` heading
     starts the next reviewer and resets the comment counter to N.1. -->

# Reviewer 1

::: {.comment summary="sample size justified by an a priori power analysis"}
The study may be underpowered. The authors report a sample of 96 participants
but give no justification for this number. Please report a power analysis or
otherwise justify the sample size.
:::

<!-- status= takes done | partial | declined | todo. "todo" prints a render
     warning listing every unaddressed comment, which is useful while drafting;
     resolve or remove all todo replies before submitting. Nesting note: a div
     inside another div needs four colons on the outer fence — `::::` here
     because the reply contains a `.quoted` box. -->

:::: {.reply status="done"}
The reviewer is right that the original submission did not justify the sample
size. We set the target sample a priori from a power analysis, which we now
report in the Method:

::: {.quoted loc="Method, p. 6"}
A power analysis for the within-subjects comparison ($d_z = 0.35$,
$\alpha = .05$, power $= .90$) indicated a required sample of 90 participants;
we recruited 96 to allow for exclusions.
:::
::::

<!-- A `.quoted` box holds verbatim text from the revised manuscript. loc= sets
     its label, e.g. "Manuscript (Method, p. 6):". Quote the revised text so the
     editor can check the change against the tracked-changes file. -->

::: {.changes}
- **Method > Participants**: a priori power analysis added (p. 6)
:::

::: {.comment summary="central effect holds across three analytic choices"}
The spacing effect in Table 2 might depend on how trials are aggregated. Please
show that the effect is robust to reasonable alternative analyses.
:::

::: {.reply status="partial"}
The aggregation choice deserves a check, and we agree. The spacing effect holds
across the three analytic choices we considered, summarized in @tbl-robustness.
A fully nonparametric reanalysis of the trial-level data is still running; we
will add it if the editor considers it necessary, but the three analyses below
already span the alternatives the reviewer raises. The same robustness bears on
[Comment 2.1](#cmt-2-1), where Reviewer 2 asks how our estimate compares with
prior work.

<!-- Tables and figures labeled inside a reply are numbered separately from the
     manuscript's ("Response Table 1") and cross-referenced with @tbl-… / @fig-….
     They render inline inside the box; nothing floats. -->

| Analysis | Effect ($d_z$) | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Primary (mean per condition) | 0.41 | [0.20, 0.62] |
| Trimmed means (10%) | 0.38 | [0.17, 0.59] |
| Mixed-effects (trial-level) | 0.43 | [0.24, 0.61] |

: The spacing effect under three analytic choices. {#tbl-robustness}
:::

::: {.changes}
- **Results**: robustness analyses added (p. 11)
- **Supplement S2**: full analytic details and code
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Reviewer 2

::: {.comment summary="effect situated relative to prior estimates"}
How does the size of the spacing effect here compare with previous estimates in
the literature? The Discussion treats it as novel without situating it.
:::

::: {.reply status="done"}
We have added a paragraph situating our estimate against prior work. The effect
we observe ($d_z = 0.41$) sits within the range reported in earlier studies, and
the robustness analysis in [Comment 1.2](#cmt-1-2) shows the estimate is stable
across analytic choices. We have toned down the "novel" framing accordingly.
:::

::: {.changes}
- **Discussion**: paragraph relating the effect to prior estimates added (p. 14)
:::

<!-- "declined" is for requests you do not act on. Decline rarely, and give a
     reason the editor can weigh — scope, feasibility, or a different question. -->

::: {.comment}
A six-month follow-up would considerably strengthen the claims about long-term
retention. I recommend collecting one.
:::

::: {.reply status="declined"}
We see the value of a six-month follow-up and considered it seriously. For this
revision we respectfully decline to collect new data: our claims concern the
one-week interval we tested, which we now state explicitly, and a six-month
follow-up would pose a different question rather than strengthen the present one.
We name it as the natural next step in the Discussion.
:::

::: {.changes}
- **Discussion**: retention claim scoped to the tested interval; six-month
  follow-up named as future work (p. 15)
:::
